court

In Panama, the court that hears your case depends on the stage of the criminal process and the seriousness of the offence. The criminal justice system operates under an accusatory system with different types of judges involved at each stage.

During the investigation stage, your case will be overseen by a Juez de Garantías (Guarantees Judge). This judge does not decide guilt or innocence but is responsible for supervising the legality of the investigation and protecting your rights. They authorise measures such as detention, searches, and other actions requested by the prosecutor.

If your case proceeds beyond the investigation stage, it will move to trial before a Tribunal de Juicio (Trial Court). This court is responsible for hearing the evidence, examining witnesses, and delivering a verdict. Trials are conducted in Spanish and decided by professional judges rather than a jury.

If you are convicted and sentenced, aspects of your sentence may later be handled by a Juez de Cumplimiento (Sentence Enforcement Judge). This judge oversees the execution of the sentence, including conditions of detention and any administrative matters related to imprisonment.

Beyond these stages, Panama has a broader judicial hierarchy. Appeals against decisions are generally made to higher courts, such as the Tribunales Superiores (Appeal Courts) and, ultimately, the Corte Suprema de Justicia (Supreme Court), which is the highest judicial authority in the country.

Most serious criminal cases involving foreign nationals—particularly drug-related offences – are handled within this system and may involve several stages and authorities before reaching an outcome.

You will be informed by your lawyer or the court authorities which judge, or court is responsible for your case at each stage. Your lawyer is the best person to explain how your specific case will proceed through the system.

The criminal process in Panama follows a structured sequence of stages that move from investigation through to trial and sentencing. It usually begins with an arrest or the filing of a complaint, after which the Public Prosecutor’s Office (Ministerio Público) takes responsibility for directing the investigation. In the initial phase, the authorities gather evidence, identify suspects, and assess whether a criminal offence has been committed.

If sufficient evidence is found, the prosecutor will request a hearing before a Juez de Garantías (Guarantees Judge). At this stage, known as the formulación de imputación, you are formally informed of the charges against you. The judge will confirm your rights and decide whether you should remain in detention or be subject to other precautionary measures. In serious cases, particularly drug-related offences, this usually results in pre-trial detention.

Following this hearing, the case enters the formal investigation phase, during which the prosecutor continues to collect and strengthen the evidence. This may include witness statements, expert reports, and additional investigative actions. Your defence lawyer may also submit evidence and challenge the prosecution’s case during this period. This stage is subject to legal time limits, although delays and extensions are common.

Once the investigation is complete, the process moves into the intermediate phase. At this stage, the prosecutor submits a formal accusation (acusación) if they believe there is enough evidence to proceed. A judge reviews the evidence presented by both sides and decides whether the case should go to trial. The judge also determines which evidence will be allowed during the trial.

If the case proceeds, it goes to the oral trial stage before a Tribunal de Juicio (Trial Court). During the trial, the prosecution presents its case, and the defence responds. Witnesses and experts are called and examined, and all evidence is presented and tested in court. There is no jury system in Panama; instead, professional judges hear the case and make the final decision. The proceedings are conducted in Spanish, and an interpreter should be provided if needed.

At the conclusion of the trial, the judges issue a verdict, deciding whether you are guilty or not guilty based on the evidence presented. If you are found guilty, the court proceeds to the sentencing stage, where it determines the appropriate penalty depending on the seriousness of the offence and the circumstances of the case. Any time already spent in detention is normally deducted from the final sentence.

After sentencing, the case enters the sentence enforcement stage, overseen by a Juez de Cumplimiento, who monitors how the sentence is carried out until completion.

Completion of investigations

Once the formal investigation phase has been carried out, the Public Prosecutor’s Office (Ministerio Público) must decide whether there is sufficient evidence to proceed with the case. During the investigation, the prosecutor gathers and reviews all relevant material, including witness statements, documentary evidence, expert reports, and any physical evidence obtained. The defence can present its own evidence and challenge the prosecution’s findings at this stage.

The investigation is considered complete when the prosecutor determines that enough evidence has been collected either to support a formal accusation or to discontinue the proceedings. If the evidence is considered insufficient, the prosecutor may request that the case be closed and no further action taken. If, however, the prosecutor believes there is a sufficient basis for prosecution, they will move the case forward by submitting a formal accusation (acusación) against the accused.

Contacting the British Embassy in Panama

The British Embassy in Panama can offer help but will not be able to get you out of prison or get you special treatment because you’re British. Find out what help the embassy or consulate can offer.

Family and friends can contact:

the British Embassy in Panama

the Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office (FCDO) in London on +44 (0)20 7008 5000

British Embassy Panama City

Consular Section

Calle 53 Marbella, Humboldt Tower 4to piso

Ciudad de Panamá, Panamá

Tel: (507) 297-6550

Fax: (507) 297-6588

Website: www.gov.uk/government/world/panama

Working hours:

Monday to Thursday: 08:00 to 16:30 Friday: 08:00 to 13:30

Visits to the Embassy are by appointment only. Please call +507 297 6550 to arrange an appointment

Finding a lawyer and translator

Find a lawyer in Panama

You should carefully consider getting a local Panamanian lawyer. Discuss all costs with them in advance.

Prisoners Abroad has information on appointing a lawyer and legal aid (not specific to Panama

Private lawyers

Check the list of local English-speaking lawyers if you want to appoint your own private lawyer. Ask the British Embassy if you need a paper copy.

Private lawyers will normally ask for a cash advance on their estimated legal fees before taking on a case. Legal costs can vary significantly depending on the complexity of the case. Defendants are usually expected to cover their own legal fees, including interpretation and administrative costs.

Legal aid

If you cannot afford a private lawyer, the Panamanian government will appoint a public defender (defensor público) to represent you. Public defenders are free of charge. They are available to all defendants who do not have private legal representation. You do not usually need to apply separately, as one will be assigned automatically. You may choose to appoint a private lawyer at any time if you are able to do so.

Find a translator or interpreter in Panama

You may need a translator to help you read documents in Spanish about your case.

Do not sign any documents unless you understand them.

You might need an interpreter to help you communicate with your lawyer or at your trial, or for prison visits.

The Panamanian authorities should provide an interpreter during official proceedings, including your statement and trial. However, in practice, access may sometimes be delayed.

Interpreter services are generally provided by the court during hearings. Outside of formal proceedings, you may need to arrange and pay for a private translator.

You can search for an English-speaking translator or interpreter in Panama through the FCDO service directory or by asking the Embassy for assistance.

Search for an English-speaking translator or interpreter in Panama

What happens when you’re arrested in Panama

You can be arrested and taken to a local police station:

because of an existing arrest warrant

where there are grounds for issuing an arrest warrant

if you’re caught in the act of performing a crime

if it’s expected you’ll leave the country to escape justice

your identity cannot be confirmed

The police must tell you in English (or a language you understand):

why you’ve been arrested

that initial proceedings against you have started

your rights

Do not sign any documents unless you understand them - you must be given an interpreter if you ask for one.

Your rights

You have the right to:

remain silent until you have legal advice

request a lawyer (private or public defender)

ask for an interpreter

inform a family member or the British Embassy

receive medical attention if needed

In practice:

you may not have immediate access to a lawyer or interpreter, especially in drug-related cases, until shortly before giving your formal statement

you should insist on speaking to a lawyer before giving any statement

you are normally allowed one phone call, but access may depend on the facility and circumstances

You will usually be held initially a police station or temporary holding facility (for example in Ancón if arrested at the airport) before being transferred to a prison. Basic conditions vary, but you should have access to food and water.

How long you can be held for

Panamanian law states that you should be brought before a judge within a short period (usually within 24 hours), depending on availability. However, delays can occur depending on availability of judges, lawyers, and interpreters. You may remain in police custody until space is available in a remand prison.

There is no strict maximum time defined in practice for how long you may remain in police holding cells before transfer.

Personal belongings

Your personal belongings will normally be taken from you when you are arrested. Items considered evidence will be retained by the authorities. Other belongings should be listed and stored. In practice, you may not always receive a detailed ticket. Some items may be lost during transfers between facilities. Your passport will be confiscated and later transferred to the British Embassy. You cannot keep your passport in prison.

Going to court

After your arrest, you will usually appear before a judge and prosecutor. At this stage, you may be asked to give a statement. A decision will also be made about your detention.

The judge will decide whether you will:

be placed on remand (most common outcome for serious offences)

be released (rare in serious cases)

face alternative measures (for minor offences only)

You should:

have legal representation (private or public defender)

be assisted by an interpreter during hearings

note that court proceedings are conducted in Spanish

Being put on remand

You may be put on remand if you’re strongly suspected of committing an offence. This means you’ll be put in prison while you wait for the criminal investigation and trial to finish.

How long you can be on remand for

the embassy cannot routinely pay for flights, but consular staff can provide guidance on the process, help with obtaining travel documents, and signpost support where available. In some circumstances, organisations such as Prisoners Abroad may be able to offer limited practical assistance or advice, but this support is not guaranteed and does not usually extend to paying for flights

Getting a passport

Make sure your British passport is still in date. Contact the British embassy before you’re released if you need an emergency travel document for your journey home.
